I'm going through the measure's key provisions: the Legislature can amend the act by a two-thirds vote in each house, but only if the change is consistent with and furthers its purposes. I'm also checking how Section 50308(a) defines an applicable individual, as a California resident as of January 1, 2026, the tax obligation date.

I'm working through the measure's financial terms now: the 5% rate on net worth above $1 billion with a phase-in, the payment options with their deferral charge, and the exemptions for retirement accounts and directly held real property. I'm also noting how the apportionment rules and the severability clause would keep the tax in place if parts were struck down.

I'm checking the measure's conflict clause, which gives priority to whichever competing billionaire-tax measure gets more yes votes, along with the proponent's standing to defend it. I'm also looking at the reserve fund split and the annual appropriation caps, which at about $25 billion a year would stretch spending over several years, plus the bar on using these funds to cut other health and education appropriations.

I'm checking how the measure's funding is meant to be spent: the 90/10 split, and whether the "no supplanting" language stops the money from quietly replacing existing state health and education dollars. Proponents read that as a ban on substitution, while opponents say the wording is ambiguous about offsetting state cuts.

I'm looking at how the constitutional amendment overrides other provisions, letting the state tax all forms of personal property and wealth and classify taxpayers differently. I'm also noting that the act's own wording treats its taxes as outside Article XIII A's limits on property tax. Next I'm weighing the opponents' claim that the Legislature could widen the tax to all Californians by a two-thirds vote, testing it against the stated purposes.

I'm now checking whether the Legislature's two-thirds amendment power reaches the constitutional part of the measure. Under Article II, Section 10(c), a statute that changes an initiative generally needs voter approval, so the opponents' claim that lawmakers could simply expand the tax to all Californians looks weaker for the constitutional section than for the statute.

I'm checking whether the Legislature's two-thirds power actually covers the constitutional part: the LAIST piece says Prop 40 writes the tax into the Constitution, which would likely need another ballot vote to expand, while the statutory parts could be changed by a two-thirds vote. A tax expert's view is that lawmakers could tweak the structure at the margins but couldn't turn it into a recurring tax or lower the wealth threshold, so the risk of expansion looks smaller than opponents suggest, though real uncertainty remains. I'm also planning to read more of the CalMatters article on Props 41 and 42, check the official guide, and verify the claim that Prop 40 taxes retirement accounts for the first time.

I'm checking whether the measure's claim that it taxes retirement accounts for the first time holds up, since qualified pensions and IRAs are exempt while Roth IRAs above $10 million are included. I also want a source for the Prop 98 figure, and I'm looking at the opponents' $25 billion cost estimate, which seems to match an earlier version of the Stanford study.

Now I'm comparing the opponents' $25 billion lost-revenue figure from the Stanford study against the later, larger estimate from the same authors, and checking the pro side's claims about revenue and the number of billionaires affected.

I'm now checking the opponents' claim that the measure would cut health coverage for over a million Californians, which traces back to the federal reconciliation law's Medicaid changes. I'm also looking at the premium-doubling claim, which seems to rest on the expiring ACA enhanced subsidies, and I want a fact check on both.

I'm checking how the opponents' healthcare claims hold up, and whether the "blank check" spending concern is valid. I'm also weighing the tax's revenue range, roughly $28 to $30 billion on the low end and about $100 billion on the high end, along with the legal risks and the measure's severability clause. The Props 41 and 42 conflict clauses could cancel Prop 40 if they draw more yes votes, so I'm going to pull their official summaries.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

Key Findings
The California election has entered its final stretch, with the governor’s race at the top of the ticket and 52 House races that will help determine the party in control of the 120th Congress. The November 3 ballot also includes 14 state propositions—five legislative measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—the most since the November 2016 election. The 2025–26 legislative session ended in late August with a flurry of bills sent to Governor Newsom to sign or veto in September. The recent trends in job growth, consumer prices, and interest rates send mixed signals about the US and California economy.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey on topics including the November races, legislative ballot measures, and citizens’ initiatives, as well as state and national issues that was conducted September 4–September 10, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) continues to lead Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a similarly wide margin (62% to 36%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty-five percent say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote. Fifty-eight percent say that voting is more important this year than in past midterms. After reading the ballot titles and labels, majorities would vote yes on Proposition 1 (55%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (60%; Rainy Day Fund). Three other legislative ballot measures fall short of a majority.
Fifty-two percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would also vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (61%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (55%; Immunology Bond), Proposition 41 (51%; Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), and Proposition 42 (54%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Partisans vary in their support for these citizens’ initiatives. Three other citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Overwhelming majorities agree that there are too many propositions on the state ballot.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think that the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Fifty-one percent of adults and likely voters say that they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance, while 45 percent of adults and 48 percent of likely voters approve of the state legislature. Majorities of adults and likely voters report that recent price increases have caused financial hardships for their household. Seventy percent of Californians think that the state is divided into economic groups, the haves and have-nots. Majorities of adults and likely voters say that they can trust the state government in Sacramento to do what is right “only some of the time.”
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-three percent of adults and 27 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance, while 17 percent of adults and 16 percent of likely voters approve of the US Congress. Seven in ten Californians are dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care and believe that the US government is responsible for ensuring that all Americans have access to health care. Fewer than half say the major parties have a lot or some good ideas. Overwhelming majorities say they can trust the federal government to do what is right “only some of the time.”
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
The top two vote-getters in the California June primary for statewide elected offices and for federal and state legislative seats are on the November ballot. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom, who is termed out of office. There are 52 House races in California that will help determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will also decide on 14 state propositions this fall—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax measures and multibillion-dollar state bonds.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. In our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), Becerra led Hilton by 25 points (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 93 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 92 percent of Republicans favor Hilton, while independents lean toward the Democratic candidate (57% Becerra, 38% Hilton). Majorities favor Becerra over Hilton across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and in the state’s major regions except for the Central Valley (46% Becerra, 52% Hilton).
Affordability and the cost of living have been the top issue on Californians’ minds in our recent polling. Sixty-five percent of likely voters say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote (30% somewhat, 5% not too important). In our February survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/), the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability were very important to 61 percent of likely voters and to majorities across parties, regions, and demographic groups. Today, majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions hold this view. Notably, partisans are largely in agreement: 69 percent of Democrats, 65 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents say that the gubernatorial candidates’ affordability positions are very important. Becerra supporters (66%) express this opinion as often as Hilton supporters (65%). Seven in ten or more of those who live in the Inland Empire (79%) or Los Angeles (70%), those who have incomes of $40,000 to $99,999 (74%), those who have children 18 or younger in their household (74%), Latinos (71%), renters (70%), and women (70%) say the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote.
Many Californians are watching news about the gubernatorial candidates. About six in ten likely voters say they are following news about candidates for the governor’s election either very (18%) or fairly (40%) closely. By comparison, in our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten likely voters were very (23%) or fairly closely (48%) following the news about candidates in the governor’s election, including majorities across partisan groups (68% Democrats, 76% Republicans, 65% independents) and demographic groups and regions. Similar shares were closely following the news about candidates in the gubernatorial election in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (21% very, 41% fairly), while fewer were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (17% very, 33% fairly), and overwhelming majorities were in September 2021 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2021/) (40% very, 41% fairly) prior to the special election on the recall of Governor Newsom. Today, partisans vary in following the news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely (57% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 50% independents), as do Becerra and Hilton supporters (53% to 69%).
House Races. When asked about their House district race, most likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a wide margin (62% to 36%). Likely voter preferences were similar in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican) and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, likely voters’ preferences for the Democratic candidate and the Republican candidate are similar in the governor’s race and the House race. More than nine in ten Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while independents say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (59% to 36%). Majorities say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district races across demographic groups and major state regions with the exception of the Central Valley (47%).
Many Californians believe that their vote matters in the 2026 midterm election. When asked about the importance of voting this year compared to past midterm elections, 58 percent of likely voters say it is more important, 39 percent say it is about as important as in past years, and only 2 percent say voting is less important to them. Californians are more likely to say that voting in the midterm is more important to them this year than they were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (43%) and in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (52%). Today, Democratic likely voters (69%) are much more likely than Republicans (50%) and independents (45%) to say that voting in this midterm is more important this year. Majorities across the state’s regions say that voting in this midterm election is more important this year. Those who say they would vote for Democratic candidates (64%) are more likely than those supporting Republican candidates (49%) in their local House races to say that voting is more important to them this year than in past midterms.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We also gauged support for five state propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Fifty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute that authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 43 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (75% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 56% independents) and between homeowners and renters (49% to 72%). Half or more across the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the state’s rainy day fund, approved by voters in 2014 to provide funding for economic downturns; 39 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (82% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 60% independents). Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 2 across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-two percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute that repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 53 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (55% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 41% independents). Half or more would vote no across the state’s major regions.
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Thirty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment; 59 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 5 falls short of a majority across partisan groups (40% Democrats, 34% Republicans, 28% independents) and across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-three percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 51 percent would vote no. Support varies across partisan groups (33% Democrats, 61% Republicans, 43% independents) and state regions (60% Central Valley; 50% Orange/San Diego; 43% Los Angeles; 35% Inland Empire; 32% San Francisco Bay Area).
When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 9 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (5% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 1% Proposition 4; 1% Proposition 5; 1% Proposition 43). Key Findings
The California election has entered its final stretch, with the governor’s race at the top of the ticket and 52 House races that will help determine the party in control of the 120th Congress. The November 3 ballot also includes 14 state propositions—five legislative measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—the most since the November 2016 election. The 2025–26 legislative session ended in late August with a flurry of bills sent to Governor Newsom to sign or veto in September. The recent trends in job growth, consumer prices, and interest rates send mixed signals about the US and California economy.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey on topics including the November races, legislative ballot measures, and citizens’ initiatives, as well as state and national issues that was conducted September 4–September 10, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) continues to lead Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a similarly wide margin (62% to 36%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty-five percent say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote. Fifty-eight percent say that voting is more important this year than in past midterms. After reading the ballot titles and labels, majorities would vote yes on Proposition 1 (55%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (60%; Rainy Day Fund). Three other legislative ballot measures fall short of a majority.
Fifty-two percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would also vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (61%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (55%; Immunology Bond), Proposition 41 (51%; Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), and Proposition 42 (54%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Partisans vary in their support for these citizens’ initiatives. Three other citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Overwhelming majorities agree that there are too many propositions on the state ballot.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think that the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Fifty-one percent of adults and likely voters say that they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance, while 45 percent of adults and 48 percent of likely voters approve of the state legislature. Majorities of adults and likely voters report that recent price increases have caused financial hardships for their household. Seventy percent of Californians think that the state is divided into economic groups, the haves and have-nots. Majorities of adults and likely voters say that they can trust the state government in Sacramento to do what is right “only some of the time.”
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-three percent of adults and 27 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance, while 17 percent of adults and 16 percent of likely voters approve of the US Congress. Seven in ten Californians are dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care and believe that the US government is responsible for ensuring that all Americans have access to health care. Fewer than half say the major parties have a lot or some good ideas. Overwhelming majorities say they can trust the federal government to do what is right “only some of the time.”
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
The top two vote-getters in the California June primary for statewide elected offices and for federal and state legislative seats are on the November ballot. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom, who is termed out of office. There are 52 House races in California that will help determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will also decide on 14 state propositions this fall—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax measures and multibillion-dollar state bonds.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. In our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), Becerra led Hilton by 25 points (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 93 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 92 percent of Republicans favor Hilton, while independents lean toward the Democratic candidate (57% Becerra, 38% Hilton). Majorities favor Becerra over Hilton across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and in the state’s major regions except for the Central Valley (46% Becerra, 52% Hilton).
Affordability and the cost of living have been the top issue on Californians’ minds in our recent polling. Sixty-five percent of likely voters say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote (30% somewhat, 5% not too important). In our February survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/), the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability were very important to 61 percent of likely voters and to majorities across parties, regions, and demographic groups. Today, majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions hold this view. Notably, partisans are largely in agreement: 69 percent of Democrats, 65 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents say that the gubernatorial candidates’ affordability positions are very important. Becerra supporters (66%) express this opinion as often as Hilton supporters (65%). Seven in ten or more of those who live in the Inland Empire (79%) or Los Angeles (70%), those who have incomes of $40,000 to $99,999 (74%), those who have children 18 or younger in their household (74%), Latinos (71%), renters (70%), and women (70%) say the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote.
Many Californians are watching news about the gubernatorial candidates. About six in ten likely voters say they are following news about candidates for the governor’s election either very (18%) or fairly (40%) closely. By comparison, in our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten likely voters were very (23%) or fairly closely (48%) following the news about candidates in the governor’s election, including majorities across partisan groups (68% Democrats, 76% Republicans, 65% independents) and demographic groups and regions. Similar shares were closely following the news about candidates in the gubernatorial election in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (21% very, 41% fairly), while fewer were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (17% very, 33% fairly), and overwhelming majorities were in September 2021 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2021/) (40% very, 41% fairly) prior to the special election on the recall of Governor Newsom. Today, partisans vary in following the news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely (57% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 50% independents), as do Becerra and Hilton supporters (53% to 69%).
House Races. When asked about their House district race, most likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a wide margin (62% to 36%). Likely voter preferences were similar in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican) and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, likely voters’ preferences for the Democratic candidate and the Republican candidate are similar in the governor’s race and the House race. More than nine in ten Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while independents say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (59% to 36%). Majorities say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district races across demographic groups and major state regions with the exception of the Central Valley (47%).
Many Californians believe that their vote matters in the 2026 midterm election. When asked about the importance of voting this year compared to past midterm elections, 58 percent of likely voters say it is more important, 39 percent say it is about as important as in past years, and only 2 percent say voting is less important to them. Californians are more likely to say that voting in the midterm is more important to them this year than they were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (43%) and in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (52%). Today, Democratic likely voters (69%) are much more likely than Republicans (50%) and independents (45%) to say that voting in this midterm is more important this year. Majorities across the state’s regions say that voting in this midterm election is more important this year. Those who say they would vote for Democratic candidates (64%) are more likely than those supporting Republican candidates (49%) in their local House races to say that voting is more important to them this year than in past midterms.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We also gauged support for five state propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Fifty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute that authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 43 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (75% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 56% independents) and between homeowners and renters (49% to 72%). Half or more across the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the state’s rainy day fund, approved by voters in 2014 to provide funding for economic downturns; 39 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (82% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 60% independents). Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 2 across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-two percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute that repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 53 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (55% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 41% independents). Half or more would vote no across the state’s major regions.
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Thirty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment; 59 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 5 falls short of a majority across partisan groups (40% Democrats, 34% Republicans, 28% independents) and across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-three percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 51 percent would vote no. Support varies across partisan groups (33% Democrats, 61% Republicans, 43% independents) and state regions (60% Central Valley; 50% Orange/San Diego; 43% Los Angeles; 35% Inland Empire; 32% San Francisco Bay Area).
When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 9 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (5% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 1% Proposition 4; 1% Proposition 5; 1% Proposition 43). Key Findings
The California election has entered its final stretch, with the governor’s race at the top of the ticket and 52 House races that will help determine the party in control of the 120th Congress. The November 3 ballot also includes 14 state propositions—five legislative measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—the most since the November 2016 election. The 2025–26 legislative session ended in late August with a flurry of bills sent to Governor Newsom to sign or veto in September. The recent trends in job growth, consumer prices, and interest rates send mixed signals about the US and California economy.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey on topics including the November races, legislative ballot measures, and citizens’ initiatives, as well as state and national issues that was conducted September 4–September 10, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) continues to lead Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a similarly wide margin (62% to 36%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty-five percent say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote. Fifty-eight percent say that voting is more important this year than in past midterms. After reading the ballot titles and labels, majorities would vote yes on Proposition 1 (55%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (60%; Rainy Day Fund). Three other legislative ballot measures fall short of a majority.
Fifty-two percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would also vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (61%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (55%; Immunology Bond), Proposition 41 (51%; Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), and Proposition 42 (54%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Partisans vary in their support for these citizens’ initiatives. Three other citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Overwhelming majorities agree that there are too many propositions on the state ballot.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think that the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Fifty-one percent of adults and likely voters say that they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance, while 45 percent of adults and 48 percent of likely voters approve of the state legislature. Majorities of adults and likely voters report that recent price increases have caused financial hardships for their household. Seventy percent of Californians think that the state is divided into economic groups, the haves and have-nots. Majorities of adults and likely voters say that they can trust the state government in Sacramento to do what is right “only some of the time.”
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-three percent of adults and 27 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance, while 17 percent of adults and 16 percent of likely voters approve of the US Congress. Seven in ten Californians are dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care and believe that the US government is responsible for ensuring that all Americans have access to health care. Fewer than half say the major parties have a lot or some good ideas. Overwhelming majorities say they can trust the federal government to do what is right “only some of the time.”
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
The top two vote-getters in the California June primary for statewide elected offices and for federal and state legislative seats are on the November ballot. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom, who is termed out of office. There are 52 House races in California that will help determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will also decide on 14 state propositions this fall—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax measures and multibillion-dollar state bonds.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. In our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), Becerra led Hilton by 25 points (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 93 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 92 percent of Republicans favor Hilton, while independents lean toward the Democratic candidate (57% Becerra, 38% Hilton). Majorities favor Becerra over Hilton across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and in the state’s major regions except for the Central Valley (46% Becerra, 52% Hilton).
Affordability and the cost of living have been the top issue on Californians’ minds in our recent polling. Sixty-five percent of likely voters say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote (30% somewhat, 5% not too important). In our February survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/), the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability were very important to 61 percent of likely voters and to majorities across parties, regions, and demographic groups. Today, majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions hold this view. Notably, partisans are largely in agreement: 69 percent of Democrats, 65 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents say that the gubernatorial candidates’ affordability positions are very important. Becerra supporters (66%) express this opinion as often as Hilton supporters (65%). Seven in ten or more of those who live in the Inland Empire (79%) or Los Angeles (70%), those who have incomes of $40,000 to $99,999 (74%), those who have children 18 or younger in their household (74%), Latinos (71%), renters (70%), and women (70%) say the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote.
Many Californians are watching news about the gubernatorial candidates. About six in ten likely voters say they are following news about candidates for the governor’s election either very (18%) or fairly (40%) closely. By comparison, in our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten likely voters were very (23%) or fairly closely (48%) following the news about candidates in the governor’s election, including majorities across partisan groups (68% Democrats, 76% Republicans, 65% independents) and demographic groups and regions. Similar shares were closely following the news about candidates in the gubernatorial election in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (21% very, 41% fairly), while fewer were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (17% very, 33% fairly), and overwhelming majorities were in September 2021 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2021/) (40% very, 41% fairly) prior to the special election on the recall of Governor Newsom. Today, partisans vary in following the news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely (57% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 50% independents), as do Becerra and Hilton supporters (53% to 69%).
House Races. When asked about their House district race, most likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a wide margin (62% to 36%). Likely voter preferences were similar in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican) and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, likely voters’ preferences for the Democratic candidate and the Republican candidate are similar in the governor’s race and the House race. More than nine in ten Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while independents say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (59% to 36%). Majorities say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district races across demographic groups and major state regions with the exception of the Central Valley (47%).
Many Californians believe that their vote matters in the 2026 midterm election. When asked about the importance of voting this year compared to past midterm elections, 58 percent of likely voters say it is more important, 39 percent say it is about as important as in past years, and only 2 percent say voting is less important to them. Californians are more likely to say that voting in the midterm is more important to them this year than they were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (43%) and in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (52%). Today, Democratic likely voters (69%) are much more likely than Republicans (50%) and independents (45%) to say that voting in this midterm is more important this year. Majorities across the state’s regions say that voting in this midterm election is more important this year. Those who say they would vote for Democratic candidates (64%) are more likely than those supporting Republican candidates (49%) in their local House races to say that voting is more important to them this year than in past midterms.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We also gauged support for five state propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Fifty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute that authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 43 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (75% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 56% independents) and between homeowners and renters (49% to 72%). Half or more across the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the state’s rainy day fund, approved by voters in 2014 to provide funding for economic downturns; 39 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (82% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 60% independents). Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 2 across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-two percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute that repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 53 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (55% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 41% independents). Half or more would vote no across the state’s major regions.
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Thirty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment; 59 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 5 falls short of a majority across partisan groups (40% Democrats, 34% Republicans, 28% independents) and across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-three percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 51 percent would vote no. Support varies across partisan groups (33% Democrats, 61% Republicans, 43% independents) and state regions (60% Central Valley; 50% Orange/San Diego; 43% Los Angeles; 35% Inland Empire; 32% San Francisco Bay Area).
When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 9 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (5% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 1% Proposition 4; 1% Proposition 5; 1% Proposition 43). Key Findings
The California election has entered its final stretch, with the governor’s race at the top of the ticket and 52 House races that will help determine the party in control of the 120th Congress. The November 3 ballot also includes 14 state propositions—five legislative measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—the most since the November 2016 election. The 2025–26 legislative session ended in late August with a flurry of bills sent to Governor Newsom to sign or veto in September. The recent trends in job growth, consumer prices, and interest rates send mixed signals about the US and California economy.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey on topics including the November races, legislative ballot measures, and citizens’ initiatives, as well as state and national issues that was conducted September 4–September 10, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) continues to lead Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a similarly wide margin (62% to 36%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty-five percent say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote. Fifty-eight percent say that voting is more important this year than in past midterms. After reading the ballot titles and labels, majorities would vote yes on Proposition 1 (55%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (60%; Rainy Day Fund). Three other legislative ballot measures fall short of a majority.
Fifty-two percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would also vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (61%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (55%; Immunology Bond), Proposition 41 (51%; Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), and Proposition 42 (54%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Partisans vary in their support for these citizens’ initiatives. Three other citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Overwhelming majorities agree that there are too many propositions on the state ballot.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think that the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Fifty-one percent of adults and likely voters say that they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance, while 45 percent of adults and 48 percent of likely voters approve of the state legislature. Majorities of adults and likely voters report that recent price increases have caused financial hardships for their household. Seventy percent of Californians think that the state is divided into economic groups, the haves and have-nots. Majorities of adults and likely voters say that they can trust the state government in Sacramento to do what is right “only some of the time.”
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-three percent of adults and 27 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance, while 17 percent of adults and 16 percent of likely voters approve of the US Congress. Seven in ten Californians are dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care and believe that the US government is responsible for ensuring that all Americans have access to health care. Fewer than half say the major parties have a lot or some good ideas. Overwhelming majorities say they can trust the federal government to do what is right “only some of the time.”
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
The top two vote-getters in the California June primary for statewide elected offices and for federal and state legislative seats are on the November ballot. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom, who is termed out of office. There are 52 House races in California that will help determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will also decide on 14 state propositions this fall—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax measures and multibillion-dollar state bonds.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. In our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), Becerra led Hilton by 25 points (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 93 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 92 percent of Republicans favor Hilton, while independents lean toward the Democratic candidate (57% Becerra, 38% Hilton). Majorities favor Becerra over Hilton across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and in the state’s major regions except for the Central Valley (46% Becerra, 52% Hilton).
Affordability and the cost of living have been the top issue on Californians’ minds in our recent polling. Sixty-five percent of likely voters say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote (30% somewhat, 5% not too important). In our February survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/), the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability were very important to 61 percent of likely voters and to majorities across parties, regions, and demographic groups. Today, majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions hold this view. Notably, partisans are largely in agreement: 69 percent of Democrats, 65 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents say that the gubernatorial candidates’ affordability positions are very important. Becerra supporters (66%) express this opinion as often as Hilton supporters (65%). Seven in ten or more of those who live in the Inland Empire (79%) or Los Angeles (70%), those who have incomes of $40,000 to $99,999 (74%), those who have children 18 or younger in their household (74%), Latinos (71%), renters (70%), and women (70%) say the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote.
Many Californians are watching news about the gubernatorial candidates. About six in ten likely voters say they are following news about candidates for the governor’s election either very (18%) or fairly (40%) closely. By comparison, in our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten likely voters were very (23%) or fairly closely (48%) following the news about candidates in the governor’s election, including majorities across partisan groups (68% Democrats, 76% Republicans, 65% independents) and demographic groups and regions. Similar shares were closely following the news about candidates in the gubernatorial election in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (21% very, 41% fairly), while fewer were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (17% very, 33% fairly), and overwhelming majorities were in September 2021 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2021/) (40% very, 41% fairly) prior to the special election on the recall of Governor Newsom. Today, partisans vary in following the news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely (57% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 50% independents), as do Becerra and Hilton supporters (53% to 69%).
House Races. When asked about their House district race, most likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a wide margin (62% to 36%). Likely voter preferences were similar in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican) and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, likely voters’ preferences for the Democratic candidate and the Republican candidate are similar in the governor’s race and the House race. More than nine in ten Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while independents say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (59% to 36%). Majorities say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district races across demographic groups and major state regions with the exception of the Central Valley (47%).
Many Californians believe that their vote matters in the 2026 midterm election. When asked about the importance of voting this year compared to past midterm elections, 58 percent of likely voters say it is more important, 39 percent say it is about as important as in past years, and only 2 percent say voting is less important to them. Californians are more likely to say that voting in the midterm is more important to them this year than they were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (43%) and in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (52%). Today, Democratic likely voters (69%) are much more likely than Republicans (50%) and independents (45%) to say that voting in this midterm is more important this year. Majorities across the state’s regions say that voting in this midterm election is more important this year. Those who say they would vote for Democratic candidates (64%) are more likely than those supporting Republican candidates (49%) in their local House races to say that voting is more important to them this year than in past midterms.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We also gauged support for five state propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Fifty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute that authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 43 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (75% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 56% independents) and between homeowners and renters (49% to 72%). Half or more across the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the state’s rainy day fund, approved by voters in 2014 to provide funding for economic downturns; 39 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (82% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 60% independents). Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 2 across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-two percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute that repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 53 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (55% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 41% independents). Half or more would vote no across the state’s major regions.
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Thirty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment; 59 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 5 falls short of a majority across partisan groups (40% Democrats, 34% Republicans, 28% independents) and across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-three percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 51 percent would vote no. Support varies across partisan groups (33% Democrats, 61% Republicans, 43% independents) and state regions (60% Central Valley; 50% Orange/San Diego; 43% Los Angeles; 35% Inland Empire; 32% San Francisco Bay Area).
When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 9 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (5% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 1% Proposition 4; 1% Proposition 5; 1% Proposition 43). Proposition 40—the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, put on the ballot by petition—imposes a one-time state tax of 5% on the net worth of any individual who was a California resident on January 1, 2026 and whose net worth is $1 billion or more.

# What, exactly, is California's "billionaire tax"? (Spoiler: It's not an annual tax on billionaires)
## What Prop 40 does
Proposition 40—the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, put on the ballot by petition—imposes a one-time state tax of 5% on the net worth of any individual who was a California resident on January 1, 2026 and whose net worth is $1 billion or more.
Net worth is measured as of December 31, 2026, and a married couple counts as one taxpayer.
The tax phases in between $1 billion and $1.1 billion, so someone worth exactly $1 billion owes nothing and someone worth $1.1 billion owes the full 5%.
A "Yes" vote does not create an annual wealth tax.
The tax applies to the 2026 tax year only and is reported and paid with 2026 income taxes in 2027.

# What, exactly, is California's "billionaire tax"? (Spoiler: It's not an annual tax on billionaires)
## What Prop 40 does
Proposition 40—the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, put on the ballot by petition—imposes a one-time state tax of 5% on the net worth of any individual who was a California resident on January 1, 2026 and whose net worth is $1 billion or more.
Net worth is measured as of December 31, 2026, and a married couple counts as one taxpayer.
The tax phases in between $1 billion and $1.1 billion, so someone worth exactly $1 billion owes nothing and someone worth $1.1 billion owes the full 5%.
A "Yes" vote does not create an annual wealth tax.
The tax applies to the 2026 tax year only and is reported and paid with 2026 income taxes in 2027.

Billionaire Tax Explained: What Proposition 40 Would Mean for California
Implications of the One-Time Billionaire Wealth Tax for Californians
August 2026 | By the California Budget & Policy Center
Print Report
key takeaway
Prop. 40 would institute a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of billionaires to raise tens of billions in temporary revenue to address the loss of federal funding and other threats to health, nutrition, and education services, largely a result of H.R. 1 — the 2025 budget reconciliation law known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.” Prop. 40 could potentially raise tens of billions in revenue in the short-term to preserve critical services, but may also lead to some income tax revenue losses in future years to the extent that billionaires leave the state to avoid the tax.

Background
California, like many other states, is facing a number of challenges to its ability to meet the needs of its residents, including the impending impacts of the deep federal cuts to public health care and nutrition assistance (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/timeline-of-funding-cuts-to-medi-cal-and-calfresh-in-california/) and the rising costs of providing services due to inflation, an aging population with more complex needs, and the state’s ongoing housing crisis. The federal cuts to Medi-Cal alone are expected to cost the state tens of billions of dollars in lost funding and could lead to around 1.3 million Californians losing health care access by 2029-30. Meaningfully addressing these challenges will require California to raise a substantial amount of revenue (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/building-an-affordable-california-requires-public-investment/).
what is h.r. 1?
H.R. 1, the 2025 budget reconciliation law known (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/hr1-and-the-federal-budget-how-california-leaders-can-respond-to-trumps-cuts/) as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” signed by President Trump on July 4, 2025, will deeply harm Californians by cutting funding for essential health care and food assistance programs — while providing massive tax breaks to the wealthy and corporations. The spending cuts will disproportionately impact families with low incomes, immigrants, and communities of color, pushing more people into poverty and widening racial and economic inequities across the state.
Even prior to these more recent challenges, California was not generating enough revenue to meet the critical needs of all Californians through the state’s communities, evidenced by the state’s poverty rate remaining the highest in the nation (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-persistent-poverty-crisis-2024-rates-remain-alarmingly-high/). In addition to the human suffering caused by failing to ensure Californians can regularly access health care, put enough food on the table, and meet their other basic needs, such a failure dampens the state economy by preventing some individuals from fully participating in it and puts fiscal pressures on state and local governments as more households are forced to turn to costly emergency services and systems of last resort.
In the near term, Prop. 40 would likely generate tens of billions in revenue to prevent health coverage losses for Californians and stabilize the state’s health care system, and could provide additional support for nutrition assistance — which is also impacted by federal cuts — and for public education. Because the revenues would be one-time, the state would not be able to maintain these services in the future unless federal funding were fully restored or the state adopted alternative sources to raise this magnitude of revenue.
There is a strong rationale for taxing accumulated wealth — or taxing increases in wealth that currently go untaxed — given the profound wealth inequality and the vast unmet needs that exist in the state and across the country, as well as the ability of some ultrawealthy households to pay very little in income taxes as a share of their wealth.
At the same time, taxing wealth at the state level comes with some risks, particularly the potential for wealthy people to leave the state to avoid the tax, which would result in future state income tax losses if they did not return — putting at risk future funding for critical state services — and potential unknown impacts on the state economy. Prop. 40 attempts to counter that risk by applying the tax to billionaires who were California residents at the beginning of 2026, however it is likely this will be challenged in courts and the outcome is not certain.
In November, California voters will need to weigh the potential benefits of Prop. 40 against its potential tradeoffs.
Who Would Be Subject to the Tax Under Prop. 40 and How Would It Be Calculated?
Prop. 40 would institute a one-time tax on the worldwide wealth of billionaires. For the purposes of the measure, a billionaire subject to the tax could be an individual, a married couple, or a trust with net worth — as defined by the measure — above $1 billion. There are around250 billionaires in California, with over $2 trillion in total wealth (https://cabillionairetracker.org/). 1 (javascript:void(0)) Forbes tracks the daily wealth of billionaires with its “Real-Time Billionaires” list, and the California-specific data was compiled in connection with Jasper Boll, Emmanuel Saez, and Gabriel Zucman, California Billionaires: Wealth, Taxes, and Wealth Tax Revenue Estimates (https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/BSZ26CAbillionaires.pdf) (NBER Working Paper 35218, May 2026). Note: Saez is an author of Prop. 40.
The tax rate would be 5% for most billionaires, but the rate would be phased in for those with net worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion. 2 (javascript:void(0)) Specifically, the 5% rate would be reduced by 0.1 percentage point for each $2 million that the household’s net worth falls below $1.1 billion. Taxpayers would have the option of paying the full amount of the tax with their 2026 tax returns or in installments across five years, with an annual deferral charge.
Net worth is typically calculated as the total value of assets held by an individual, couple, or family minus their total debts. However, Prop. 40 allows some exclusions from the net worth calculation, including:
Real property holdings, which are subject to constitutional tax limitations due to Proposition 13, approved by California voters in 1978;
Tangible personal property — such as vehicles, jewelry, appliances, or business equipment — held outside of California; 3 (javascript:void(0)) Tangible personal property is excluded from the net worth calculation if it is held outside of California for at least 270 days during 2026 unless it was temporarily relocated for the purpose of tax avoidance. and
Certain pensions, retirement accounts, and deferred compensation arrangements.
The measure would apply the tax to billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026, and the amounts subject to the tax would be determined based on their net worth on December 31, 2026. There will likely be legal challenges to the application of the tax based on residency prior to the enactment of the tax. Federal and state tax measures often have retroactivity provisions to minimize tax avoidance and courts have upheld many of these laws, although it is unknown how courts would ultimately rule on this measure. The measure specifies that in the case the residency and valuation dates are invalidated by courts, these dates shall be construed to be the earliest dates consistent with law.
Prop. 40 establishes procedures for estimating the value of various types of assets that would be included in net worth for the purpose of the tax. Valuation is simple for some assets, such as holdings of publicly traded stock, which have a known market value at any given time. Other assets, such as shares of private businesses, intellectual property such as copyrights or trademarks, and artwork, are more difficult to value without a sale taking place. The measure has detailed valuation rules and formulas for different types of assets, and both the taxpayer and the state’s Franchise Tax Board — which would be responsible for administering the tax — could obtain certified appraisals in the case of valuation disputes. Additionally, the measure contains provisions intended to minimize the ability of taxpayers to avoid or evade their tax responsibility. 4 (javascript:void(0)) Tax avoidance reflects legal avenues to reducing tax liability, such as redirecting wealth holdings to exempted assets or relocating, whereas tax evasion encompasses illegal tactics to avoid taxes, such as hiding assets in tax havens, underreporting of asset values, or falsely claiming residency outside of the tax jurisdiction.
Example: Potential Impact of Prop. 40 on Mark Zuckerberg
Mark Zuckerberg, cofounder of Facebook, has a net worth of around $200 billion (https://www.forbes.com/profile/mark-zuckerberg/?ctpv=rtb&list=rtb). Assuming he has approximately $200 billion in wealth subject to Prop. 40 on December 31, 2026, when net worth is to be determined for the purpose of the measure, he would owe around $10 billion in tax, which he could pay in five annual installments of $2 billion. His remaining wealth of around $190 billion would still be more than the entire economies of dozens of countries, roughly on par with (https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.MKTP.CD?most_recent_value_desc=true) the Gross Domestic Product of Morocco.
For comparison, Zuckerberg’s net worth increased 175% from 2023 to 2024 (https://www.forbes.com/profile/mark-zuckerberg/?ctpv=rtb&list=rtb) according to Forbes data, from $64.4 billion to $177 billion.
What Is the Difference Between Income and Wealth?
Capital Gains: Increases in Wealth
Households holding assets that have increased in value pay federal and state tax on those gains only when they sell those assets. This is known as a realized capital gain.
However, the value of an asset can grow exponentially and go untaxed as long as it is held onto — an unrealized capital gain. While the household doesn’t directly receive the proceeds from the gain until selling the asset, unrealized capital gains represent an increase in the household’s wealth and financial well-being (https://www.cbpp.org/research/federal-tax/arguments-against-taxing-unrealized-capital-gains-of-very-wealthy-fall-flat).
For ultra-wealthy households, unrealized capital gains make up a large share of their total wealth. 5 (javascript:void(0)) For example, the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy estimated (https://itep.org/the-geographic-distribution-of-extreme-wealth-in-the-u-s/#:~:text=This%20ratio%20increases%20at%20higher%20levels%20of%20wealth%2C%20with%20unrealized%20gains%20making%20up%20almost%2070%20percent%20of%20billionaire%20wealth.) that unrealized capital gains represent nearly 70% of total wealth for billionaires. In some cases, ultra-wealthy households — such as corporate founders — can avoid paying income taxes entirely in some years by not taking a salary, not selling any stocks or other assets, and simply borrowing against their wealth to pay their bills. There is evidence of some of the wealthiest Americans engaging in this behavior, detailed in analyses of leaked tax returns by investigative journalists (https://www.propublica.org/article/the-secret-irs-files-trove-of-never-before-seen-records-reveal-how-the-wealthiest-avoid-income-tax), although recent research suggests (https://taxpolicycenter.org/taxvox/richs-real-tax-trick-isnt-buy-borrow-die) that this is not a widespread phenomenon and that overall, wealthy households do have significant taxable income and their incomes allow them to cover their expenses while continuing to invest and grow their wealth.
Additionally, if someone holds onto assets until their death, their heirs do not have to pay any tax on the gain due to a provision in both federal and state law known as “stepped-up basis (https://www.pgpf.org/article/what-is-the-stepped-up-basis-and-how-does-it-affect-the-federal-budget/),” estimated to cost California around $5 billion each year. 6 (javascript:void(0)) Department of Finance, Tax Expenditure Report: 2025-26 (https://dof.ca.gov/media/docs/forecasting/revenue-and-taxation/tax-expenditure-reports/2025-26-Tax-Expenditure-Report.pdf), p. 24. Note that the estimated annual cost of the provision is not equivalent to the revenue that could be generated from repealing it, and for this provision the revenue gains from repeal would start in the low hundreds of millions (https://lao.ca.gov/LAOEconTax/Article/Detail/797#:~:text=Eliminate%20Capital%20Gains%20Step%2DUp%20Basis%20on%20Inherited%20Assets.) and increase with time, potentially reaching $5 billion annually in the future. Essentially, the combination of unrealized capital gains not being taxed and stepped-up basis results in some large wealth increases never being taxed.
How Is Wealth Distributed Across California?
Across the country, the gaps in income (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/scf/dataviz/scf/chart/#range:1989,2022;series:Before_Tax_Income;demographic:inccat;population:all;units:median) and wealth (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/scf/dataviz/scf/chart/#range:1989,2022;series:Net_Worth;demographic:nwcat;population:all;units:median) have steadily grown with the top 10% of households seeing substantial growth in both income and wealth accumulation. Similarly, in California, only a tiny fraction of the population benefits from extreme income and wealth.
While both wealth and income inequality are prevalent in the state, wealth is even more unequally distributed (https://www.ppic.org/publication/wealth-in-california/#:~:text=%C2%A0This%20difference%20is%20higher%20than%20in%20the%20rest%20of%20the%20country%2C%20where%20the%2080th%20percentile%20is%2099%20times%20the%2020th%2C%20and%20higher%20than%20income%20inequality%20in%20California.) than income in California. While the state has more wealth than the rest of the country (https://www.ppic.org/publication/wealth-in-california/), the disparities in wealth are also starkest in California.
When focusing on the wealth distribution in the state, the data show an alarming gap between households with high and low wealth. Specifically, the wealthiest 20% of households have a net worth of over $1.5 million (https://www.ppic.org/publication/wealth-in-california/#:~:text=High%20net%20worth%20households%20have%20substantially%20more%20wealth%20than%20low%20net%20worth%20households.), while the bottom 20% of households have a net worth of $13,000 or less. Those who would be subject to the Prop. 40 tax — those with a net worth above $1 billion — have a net worth of over 3,000 times the median household.
Wealth is also unequally distributed across racial and ethnic groups. For example, the median net worth of white households in 2023 was almost ten times (https://www.ppic.org/publication/wealth-in-california/#:~:text=Net%20worth%20is%20highest%20among%20older%2C%20college%2Deducated%2C%20and%20white%20and%20Asian%20households.) the median net worth of Latinx households, reflecting the historical barriers to wealth accumulation (https://apps.urban.org/features/wealth-inequality-charts/) these communities have faced. Black, Latinx, and other households of color often have less wealth due to many factors including a lower likelihood of owning stocks (https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/03/06/a-booming-us-stock-market-doesnt-benefit-all-racial-and-ethnic-groups-equally/), occupational segregation (https://www.americanprogress.org/article/occupational-segregation-in-america/) pushing them into lower-payer jobs, and a lack of inherited generational wealth (https://budgetmodel.wharton.upenn.edu/p/2021-12-17-inheritances-by-race/). These factors likely contribute to the large wealth disparities that have persisted throughout history.
How Much Revenue Will Prop. 40 Raise?
There is a high degree of uncertainty in estimating the potential revenue from this measure since it is impossible to accurately predict how billionaires and the courts will respond to the tax. It is likely there will be some avoidance and evasion of the tax, as billionaires may hide or underreport their assets, shift their asset holdings toward those that are exempt from the tax, attempt to sever their ties with California, or engage in other tactics to minimize or eliminate their tax liability.
After attempting to account for these factors, the Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) that the billionaire tax would likely raise “tens of billions” of dollars in the near term. Billionaire Tax Explained: What Proposition 40 Would Mean for California
Implications of the One-Time Billionaire Wealth Tax for Californians
August 2026 | By the California Budget & Policy Center
Print Report
key takeaway
Prop. 40 would institute a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of billionaires to raise tens of billions in temporary revenue to address the loss of federal funding and other threats to health, nutrition, and education services, largely a result of H.R. 1 — the 2025 budget reconciliation law known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.” Prop. 40 could potentially raise tens of billions in revenue in the short-term to preserve critical services, but may also lead to some income tax revenue losses in future years to the extent that billionaires leave the state to avoid the tax.
